4.14.11 Size Dimension
a. Area:
i.

The area of a sign face (which is also the sign area of a wall sign or other sign with only one
face) shall be computed by means of the smallest rectangle that will encompass the limits of the
writing, emblem, or other display, together with any material or color forming an integral part of
the background of the display or used to differentiate the sign from the backdrop or structure
against which it is placed, but not including any supporting framework, base, bracing or
decorative fence or wall when such fence or wall otherwise meets the regulations of this chapter
and is clearly incidental to the display itself. Street address numbers are not included within the
sign copy area.

ii. In the case of signs mounted back-to-back only one side of the sign is to be used for computation
of the area. Back-to-back signs shall be defined as double-faced signs. The maximum angle of a
double-faced sign shall be 45 degrees, except for signs located at corners in which case the
angle may be 90 degrees. Otherwise, the surface area of each sign is to be separately
computed.
iii. For a single wall, all pieces of information or other graphic representations within a grouping on
that wall shall be measured as though part of one sign, encompassed within one rectangle,
which may not exceed the permitted total wall area to which the sign is affixed. For a single wall
on a multi-occupant building, the area of signs shall be computed using these principles and the
aggregate copy of each individual sign shall not exceed the allowed percentage of the total wall
area to which the sign(s) is affixed.
iv. This diagram illustrates how sign area is measured:

b. Height:
The height of a sign shall be the vertical distance from the mean grade elevation taken at the
fronting street side of a structure to the highest point of a sign or supporting structure.

4.14.12 Illumination
a. Neon:
i.

Neon is allowed for wall signs or projecting signs only. Neon must be affixed to a sign backing.

ii. Lettering or logos directly hanging on the fascia of the building are prohibited.
iii. Neon may only be utilized for the name of the principle use, with minimal ancillary lettering or logo
incorporated into the sign face.
iv. One (1) Neon sign per building is allowed, and is limited to 0.5 sq. ft. per 1 linear foot of wall
space. Any additional signage allowed (Wall Signs) must be non-illuminated.
v. Neon is prohibited for any use other than specific lettering or logo signage. Architectural neon
lighting (for example outlining windows) is prohibited.
b. Exterior Illumination:
i.

If Illumination is external, it shall be located and directed solely at the sign.

ii. The light source shall not be visible from or cast into the right-of-way, or cause glare hazards to
pedestrians, motorists, or adjacent properties.
iii. The light source shall not be mounted to any part of the sign.
iv. Only one exterior light shall be permitted per sign face for signs 16 square feet or less, and two
exterior lights for sign faces that exceed 16 square feet in size.
c. Interior Illumination:
i.

A Channel Illuminated Sign is a sign whose light source is located in the interior of a sign so that light
illumination shines through the front surface of the sign in specific “cut-away” areas. Any words,
lettering, figures, numerals, emblems, devices, trademarks, or trade names, or any combination
thereof, by which anything is made known and which is designed to attract attention and/or convey a
message, may be displayed by channel cutting the words, letters, figures, etc. out of the surface of
the sign. The sign itself is illuminated through cuts, or channels made through the surface of the sign.

ii. A push-thru acrylic sign is typically an internally illuminated sign with letters and/or logos cut out of
translucent acrylic that is as thick or thicker than the opaque sign face material, and mounted on the
inside of the sign face so that the acrylic material’s thickness extends flush with our pushing through
and beyond the front plane of the sign face. Acrylic letters are raised from the surface of the sign
face so that light passes through the edges. Acrylic that extends beyond the front plane may also
have a face of all letters/logos to create a back light effect if desired.
iii. A maximum of 10 foot candles is permitted on any portion of the sign. A foot candle is defined as a unit
of luminance or light falling onto a surface. It stands for the light level on a surface one foot from a
standard candle.
iv. All lighting shall meet all applicable electrical codes.

4.14.13 Alternative Signage Plans
An Alternative Signage Plan may be used where impractical situations would result from this code.
Alternative locations, size or quantity may be justified due to topography, utility easements, lot
configuration or subdivision (particularly with respect to a shopping center), or location and size of preexisting development. Also, the proposed use or collection of uses may not be captured by the spirit
and intent of this code, justifying an Alternative Signage Plan. The Planning Commission shall approve
an Alternative Signage Plan if it meets the purpose and intent of the sign code. The following
conditions shall be met in order for an Alternative Signage Plan to be considered for approval:
a. The applicant must show that installation of signage per this code while meeting other site-specific
constraints as listed above would put the site in direct violation of other City Ordinances or State or
Federal regulations, under any practical site layout configuration.
b. The use(s) and/or architectural elements proposed for the site (as already approved by the Planning
Department) are such that a standard sign plan under this code would be considered not in keeping
with the code.
4.14.14 Electronic Message Signs
a. Sign Type: Electronic message signs shall only be allowed on monument mounted and pole signs.
b. Size: The maximum sign area of the electronic portion of an electronic message sign shall not
exceed 50 square feet.
c. Dimming and Brightness: Signs shall be equipped with dimming technology that automatically
adjusts the display brightness based on ambient light conditions. The sign shall not exceed 0.3 foot
candles illumination above ambient light level.
d. Movement: The illusion of movement by means of a preprogrammed (repetitious or sequential)
switching action in which illuminated elements of the sign are turned off or on to visually simulate the
impression of motion characteristic of chasing, running, blinking, oscillating, twinkling, scintillating, or
expanding and contracting light patterns, is prohibited.
e. Rate of Change: No electronic message sign shall change copy more frequently than once during
any eight (8) second intervals. Electronic message signs that only display the time, temperature, or
both the time and the temperature, may change at real time.
f.

Allowable Zones: As allowed by the MONUMENT SIGN & PYLON SIGN Section of this Code.

4.14.15 Maintenance
All sign(s)/sign structure and premises surrounding the same shall be maintained by the owner thereof in
a clean, sanitary condition and free and clear of all rubbish and weeds. All components thereof,
including supports, braces, anchors, etc., shall be kept in compliance with all building and electrical
codes, and in conformance with the requirements of this Code. All components should be free from
deterioration, termite infestation, rot, rust or loosening. Repair and replacement of any faded, peeled,
cracked or otherwise damaged or broken parts of a sign is required by this Code.
4.14.16 Violations
a. When a violation of the sign code exists, the Code Official shall notify the alleged violator. The
notification should specify those sections of the sign code which the individual may be in violation of
and shall state that the individual has seven (7) days from the date of the notification in which to
correct the alleged violation or appear in court. In the case of a prohibited sign, the Code Official
shall, if possible, remove such sign and notify the alleged violator. If violation continues, the alleged
violator will be issued a citation.
b.

If, upon inspection, the Code Official finds that a sign is abandoned or structurally, materially, or
electrically defective in such a way that it endangers the public, the Code Official shall notify the
owner of the building/property stating the nature of the violation and requiring them to remove the
endangerment immediately and to repair or remove the sign within thirty (30) days of the date of
notification or appear in court. In case of emergency, the Code Official may cause the immediate
removal of a dangerous or defective sign without notice. Signs removed in this manner must present
a hazard to the public safety and defined in the local building codes or traffic codes.

4.14.17 Removal & Revocation by the Code Official
The Code Official may cause the removal of an illegal sign, and/or the revocation of an issued sign
permit under any of the following circumstances and at any time.
a. Misleading. The City determines that information in the application was materially false or misleading;
b. Conformity to Application. The Sign as installed does not conform to the Sign permit application;
c. Violation of Code. The Sign violates this Code, the zoning ordinance, building code, or other applicable law,
regulation, or ordinance; or
d. Maintenance and Abandonment. The Code Official determines that the Sign is not being properly maintained
or has been abandoned.
i.

After removal of the sign, a notice shall be mailed to the sign owner stating the nature of the work
and the date of which it was performed and demanding payment of the cost as certified by the
Code Official. If the amount specified in the notice is not paid within sixty (60) days of the notice,
it shall become an assessment upon a lien against the property of the sign owner, and will be
certified as an assessment against the property.
ii. If a business discontinues the use of a site associated with a particular sign, the sign display
area, housing, and any means to permanently affix said sign, shall collectively be considered
‘abandoned’ by the Code Official.
• Abandoned signs, associated appurtenances, and means to permanently affix, shall
be fully removed within sixty (60) days of receipt of a duly served notice of violation.
It shall be the responsibility of the landowner to ensure all signage as described
above is removed from the site.

Cabot City Council Work Session
Cabot City Annex / Council Chambers
January 6, 2020
6:30 p.m.
The Cabot City Council held its monthly Work Session on Monday, January 6, 2020
in the City Annex Council Chambers. Council members present were: Ed Long,
James Reid, Damon Bivins, Ronald Waymack, Doug Warner, Kevin Davis, Norma
Naquin and Matt Webber. Others present: Mayor Ken Kincade, City Attorney Ben
Hooper, City Clerk & Treasurer Tammy Yocom, Deputy City Clerk Lisa Milam.
Mayor Kincade called the meeting to order at 6:30 p.m. Matt Webber led the
Pledge of Allegiance and Mayor Kincade led the opening prayer.
Motion to read legislation by title only by Kevin Davis, second by Ron Waymack.
Motion passed by a unanimous vote.
Municipal Services Committee Business:
1. Resolution No. 1 of 2020 – A RESOLUTION TO AUTHORIZE THE MAYOR
AND CITY CLERK/TREASURER TO ENTER INTO A CONTRACT WITH JCB OF
ARKANSAS FOR THE PURCHASE OF A 2019 JOHN DEERE 6105E TRACTOR;
AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES was read by City Clerk/Treasurer Tammy
Yocom. Discussion. Motion to adopt by Ed Long, second by Norma Naquin.
Motion passed with a unanimous Roll Call Vote.
2. Community Cats Proposed Ordinance - Discussion. No action.
3. Amended Sign Code - Discussion. James Reid requested the “red-line”
version. Mayor Kincade requested this legislation be codified soon. No
action.
4. Ordinance No. 1 of 2019 – Discussion. It was determined City Attorney, Ben
Hooper will write the council organizational legislation for 2020 and council
will make changes during the next council meeting. No vote taken. Ben
asked the council to determine when they will meet again since the regularly
scheduled meeting falls on a Holiday. Motion to move the January Council
Meeting to January 27th by Norma Naquin, second by James Reid. Motion
passed with a unanimous Roll Call Vote.
5. Resolution No. 3 of 2020 – A RESOLUTION TO AUTHORIZE THE MAYOR
AND CITY CLERK/TREASURER TO ENTER INTO A CONTRACT WITH REGAL
RESTORATION FOR THE CABOT PUBLIC LIBRARY ROOF REPLACEMENT;
TO AMEND THE 2020 SENIOR CITIZENS CENTER/HEALTH/LIBRARY
MAINTENANCE FUND BUDGET AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES was read by
City Clerk/Treasurer Tammy Yocom. Discussion. Motion to adopt by Matt
Webber, second by James Reid. Motion passed with a unanimous Roll Call
Vote.
6. Municipal Services Community Input - None
Police & Fire Committee Business:

116

1. Resolution No. 2 of 2020 – A RESOLUTION TO ADOPT THE 2020
FRANCHISE FEE BONDS/CAPITAL PROJECTS – CENTRAL FIRE STATION
FUND BUDGET; AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES was read by City
Clerk/Treasurer Tammy Yocom. Discussion. Motion to adopt by Ed Long,
second by Norma Naquin. Motion passed with a unanimous Roll Call Vote.
2. Police & Fire Community Input – None
Budget & Personnel Committee Business:
1. Budget & Personnel Committee Input – Discussion on who takes the Mayor’s
place in his absence. Mayor Kincade announced “just for the record,
Tammy Yocom is my replacement at City Hall”. City Attorney, Ben Hooper,
explained “the Mayor has two people who replace him in his absence for
each set of his duties. One for his administrative duties, which will be
Tammy, and one for his legislative duties which is presiding over meetings
and that is the one you guys will pick.” No action.
2. Budget & Personnel Committee Business: None
Community Development Committee Business:
1. Quarterly Report – Amy Williams, President/CEO Cabot Chamber of
Commerce gave a verbal report on the fourth quarter of 2019 Economic
Development. A copy of her talking points are attached to these minutes.
Discussion on the payment to the Chamber for the 2020 Economic
Development Contract. City Attorney Ben Hooper explained the invoice for
$100,000 from the Chamber immediately threw up a red flag with him since
the contract doesn’t mention an amount at all. We need something to
justify a $100,000 payment since the contract doesn’t mention the amount
or even making a payment up front. Kevin Davis recommended resolving
the issue somehow because the City has made a payment to the Chamber
in the past. He suggested running it by Municipal League.
2. McKinstry Energy Report Presentation – Jay Holstead with McKinstry Energy
presented a Power Point presentation. Please see attached for a printed
copy of the presentation.
3. Community Development Input - None
Military Affairs Committee Business:
1. Military Affairs Committee Community Input - None
Meeting was adjourned at 9:15 p.m. by a unanimous vote.

the City of Cabot Work Session held on Monday, January 6, 2020 at 6:30 p.m.

Cabot Parks and Recreation Commission Meeting
December 17, 2019
Cabot Veterans Park Meeting Room
508 North Lincoln, Cabot, Arkansas 72023

I.

Call to Order/Roll Call
Maggie Cope called the meeting to order at 6:31 pm.
Present: Maggie Cope, Greg Sled, Nick Whitaker, Tricia Ambeau, Adam Nobles.
Guests: Greg Crumpton, Doug Warner, Jeff Green

II.

Minutes of Regular Meeting
The minutes of the regular meeting held on October 15, 2019 were presented. GREG SLED
MOTIONED TO ACCEPT THE MINTES OF OCTOBER 15, 2019, SECOND BY NICK WHITAKER, ALL
SAY AYE.
Financials

III.

October and November 2019 financials were presented. TRICIA AMBEAU MOTIONED TO ACCEPT THE
FINANCIALS AS PRESENTED, SECOND BY ADAM NOBLES. General Director Travis Young stated the
months ended well. There was an overage due to correcting several maintenance issues at the
community center. Staff uniforms were purchased, and tablets were ordered for staff to enter time in
and out for payroll. Additional pay period from softball fell into November. Matching funds from a
grant for trail lights on Richie Road were also paid out. Assigner fees paid double due to all the rainouts.
Numbers are down by about 50 players in youth basketball due to teams leaving the rec league for
travel ball. ALL SAY AYE.

IV.

Programs
Program Director Lorenzo Mendoza reported the basketball preseason tournaments were
played last weekend. Games are going well and will stop for two weeks due to the holidays and
resume the second week of January. Spring sports registration, baseball, softball, soccer,
volleyball, and tennis will begin January 20th.
BMX – The last race of the season was held the weekend before Thanksgiving. Glue was but
down on the track and more dirt was added Racing will resume when the weather warms. The
group had 30 riders represent at the Grands.
Flag Football – The group reported a great season and still has a couple of purchases to make
for the spring season, paying insurance and replacing some equipment for around $7500.00. A
tournament held in November was represented well and a trophy was brought back to Cabot.
The commission asked if there were any plans for the money since they have a high balance left
in their account. They talked about donating to some charity groups. The group stated that

120

some of the money not paid out was due to rainouts over the last two seasons and not having
to pay referees and purchasing equipment, which is typically about $20, 000.00 per year. They
would like to arrange to play more games, but the biggest obstacle is not having enough
referees available to add more games.
Cabot Football Association – Did not hold a meeting last month. Held board elections and have
about the same board as last season but missing the Director of Scheduling.
V.

Construction/Facility Update
General Director Travis Young gave an update on facilities. Two sugar maples were donated for
the Community Pond Park. The floors at the community center were waxed and buffed and the
gym walls were painted. The lights around the walking track have yet to be updated. The turfs
on the fields are 100% completed. Any ruts created will be repaired by GEO. The maintenance
shop has been completed. The walking trails had new LED lights installed and the trails will be
resealed. Comp hours were held to 160 at most. We were not awarded the Outdoor Recreation
matching grants this year as we have the last couple of years. The trails at Regional Park are
coming along well with one boundary line issue being looked at for the proposed trail system at
the Regional Park.

VI.

Old Business
ASE Contract/Rates – The commission had asked Greg Crumpton to look over the contract. No
discussion followed. The commission discussed the way different tournaments were operated
around the area. Most cities have a cleanup fee up to $1000.00 per day, some did away with
the fee. Paying clean up fees per field will be discussed with the tournament director. Make
sure we stock heavily with field dry as to not cancel a tournament. General Director Travis
Young stated that we need to lock in the dates for tournaments with Will Roark. NICK
WHITAKER MOTIONED TO APPROVE AGREED ON AMOUNT THAT WILL ROARK AND GENERAL
DIRECTOR TRAVIS YOUNG DECIDE UPON PER FIELD, PER DAY, TO INCLUDE CLEANUP, SECOND
BY GREG SLED. ALL SAY AYE.

VII.

New Business
Audit – No issues were noted. Clean audit. Jeff Green gave the commission a summary of the
audit.

121

4th of July Celebration – The 4th falls on a Saturday this year and staff would like to get a date
set for the celebration in order to secure fireworks and start the planning process. July 2nd or
3rd are the dates suggested. Other cities around Cabot have already scheduled for the 4th. NICK
WHITAKER MOTIONED TO HOLD THE CELEBRATION ON JULY 3RD, SECOND BY ADAM NOBLES,
ALL SAY AYE.
Budget – General Director Travis Young discussed items in our budget. A&P tax should give us
75% of taxes collected. There is about $125,000.00 that we are missing by not receiving that
75%. Mr. Young stated he will ask questions about this issue at the next A&P meeting and will
give the commission an update. The numbers are pretty much hard numbers. Salaries for
employees were looked at. Four employees are topped out on the pay scale and will only
receive cost of living increase. Those four employees will receive a onetime check to cover the
cost of living instead of spreading the amount out through the year. NICK WHITAKER
MOTIONED TO APPROVE THE 2020 BUDGET AS PRESENTED. Mr. Young stated that our
beverage contract is up this year and will go out for proposals between Pepsi and Coke
Companies. A display board for the community center will be purchased with the money
received from the chosen company. Discussion lead to adding a therapeutic coordinator to
budget to head up programs for special needs children and adults. It will add about $52,000.00
a year to the budget if a full-time person is hired, a part-time position may be possible.
Discussion was held due the motion on the table, SECOND BY TRICIA AMBEAU. Discussion
continued. Tricia Ambeau stated that she had spoken with Mr. Young about adding a
Therapeutic Coordinator to staff to head the program. This may include after school programs,
sports and a variety of activities. We would need to research the needs in the community. Ten
percent of the school’s population is special needs, and this does not include adults. The need
for programs in the community is there. The commission would like to put a plan together
within the next three to six months and capture the surrounding communities in the plan. ALL
IN FAVOR OF PASSING THE 2020 BUDGET AS PRESENTED, ALL SAY AYE.
Lifeguard incentive – Lifeguards will work a certain number of hours and be reimbursed for
class cost if they commit certain hours to a full outdoor season. Incentives will be based from
1-year guards to 4-year guards. One half of the lifeguards that we currently certify go to other
pools to work. GREG SLED MOTIONED TO ACCEPT STAFF RECOMMENTION FOR THE
INCENTIVE FOR REIMBURSEMENT, SECOND BY ADAM NOBLES, ALL SAY AYE.
Officer elections – Per the bylaws of Cabot Parks and Recreation Commission, the officers shall
be chosen at the December meeting each year, the board shall select a Chairman and a Co-

sidewalk requirements along the proposed interior road. As such, the
preliminary plat will need revisions based on the outcome of this
request,
 If approved, additional notations on the plat specifying the
waivers requested, code reference, as date approved;
 If not approved or partially approved, adjust roadway cross
sections as applicable based on degree of waivers applied to the
project
UDC Section 5.5.2 regarding required half-street improvements may
only be waived if one or two conditions are met. 1) The development
entails four lots or less; or 2) The public roadway is not slated for
future improvement. Given that the State Statute allows Cities’ to
plan and implement improvements in their defined Planning Area
Boundary, requiring half-street improvements in line with adopted
Mater Street Plan is warranted here. This is especially the case given
that an increase in development beyond the ‘Phase 1’ (as platted) area
is likely in the future, which will result in increased utilization of the
local road onto the minor arterial (Mt. Tabor Road). Otherwise, an Inlieu contribution may be requested to Municipal Services; Temporary
easement must be placed on preliminary plat for purposes of
fire/safety apparatus to service the lots as platted; water service
confirmation letter from Grand Prairie Bayou prior to final plat
approval; unless the applicant can demonstrate otherwise, the use of
ADS (HDPE) materials may not be used to convey stormwater
underneath roadway. AS recommended by engineering review,
reinforced concrete should be utilized instead, and noted as such on
the plans street layout and cross section; plans must be revised to
show the installation of additional inlets upstream from Mt. Tabor
Road; move fire hydrant at the end of lot 17 to the lot line between lot
15 and lot 17; sheet 3 of 5/ Street Profile must be changed and edited
accordingly from 50’ to 60’ R/W.

City Council Meetings

1,

Meetin:

The City Council shall meet in regular session on the third Monday of each month at 7:00 PM.
When a hoilday occurs on any such Monday, the regular meeting shall be held on the following
Mondaa at the same hour unless otherwise proivided by motion. The regular meeting time may
be rescheduled by the City Council in special circumstances, but when so done the change must
be made far enough in advance to allow normal public notifications.

Location

The place of City Council meetings shall be in the Cabot City Annex unless another place has
been previously set by the City Council.

Work Session

Work sessions provide Council Members the opportunity to meet with staff in order to inquire
about complex issues, discuss solutions and alternatives,and thhe finalize agenda. Work sessions
may be used by councilmembers to prepare for upcoming regular meetings. These meetings are
less formal and are often used for information gathering; no formal votes are taken.
However, it should be noted that work sessions are subject to the open meetings law.
DISCUSSION NEEDED ON VOTING—yes or no

Special Meetings

Special meetings may be called by three or more Council Members or the Mayor. Notification of
a special meeting, including specific items to be considered, shall be at least two hours prior to
the meeting.

Executive Session
An executive session may be requested by any member of the City Council. A majortiy vote of
by the City Council to convene in excecutive session. Executive sessions will be permitted only

for the purpose of considering the employment, appointement, promotion, demotion, disciplining,
or resignation or any public officer or employee.

Addition of Agenda Items at City Council Meeting

Any member of the City Council or the Mayor may add an item to the agenda. However, they
should strive to always have thier item/items included on the work session agenda. A new item
added to the Council Agenda after the work session meeting should only be considered if it
required immediate City Council action. The City Council may only place such new item on the
City Council meeting’s agenda by suspending the rules by two-thirds vote.

Readings

suspend the rules.
If the emergency clause is requested, the reason shall be clearly stated witin the “emergency
clause” section of the ordinance, or it will not be considered by Council.

Council Committees

Each Council Committee shall have three or four members each, newly appointed January or”
each year. Appointments shall be per written request to the City Attorney, Council Member shall
list his/her top three committtee. When appointments are made should there be any conflict,
senority shall prevail. Every Council Member shall serve on a minimum of one committee. Each
committee shall elect a chair and vice chair during the first committee meeting.

Committee Meetings

Committee Meetings shall be held when possible at times that allow all members of the
committee to attend. In order for a committee to make an official recommendation to the City
Council, a majority of the committee members must agree on that recommendation. Council
Members who are not of the particular committee meeeting, but are in attendance, shall do so

10. Mayor Realtionship

In exercising its management responsibilities, the City Council reserves its authority to
approve policy which represents broad statements of its intentions, approves plans and
programs, and delegate authority of administration to the Mayor, except those rights
that are by law conferred upon or reserved to the city council. The City Council
delegates the authority of the Mayor to hire capable personnel within an approved
wage and salary policy, to plan and establish schedules and to train, supervise and
terminate employees. Per A.C.A. § 14-42-110, the City Council reserves the authority to
review the hiring or removal of a department head and may overturn the hiring or
removal of a department head by the Mayor upon two-thirds majority of the total
membership of the City Council

Definition of responsibilities.

(1) The Mayor has the principal responsibility for directing the operations of the city
government and for advising and assisting the City Council in its deliberations. In
connection with the latter responsibility, the City Council expects and requests the Mayor to
furnish it with whatever data, information, and material it may need to properly carry out its
functions in an informed manner.

AGREEMENT WITH THE CABOT CHAMBER OF COMMERCE AND TO WAIVE

WHEREAS, the Cabot City Council recognizes the need for economic development within
and for the City; and

WHEREAS, the City of Cabot and the Cabot Chamber of Commerce have met and
discussed the Economic Development Services Agreement and find it to be in the best interest of
the general public; and

WHEREAS, the City of Cabot acknowledges the excellent performance by the Cabot
Chamber of Commerce and because of the specialized and valuable information and the
understanding of the economic development needs, formal competitive bidding is not practical and
the City of Cabot wishes to waive competitive bidding; and

WHEREAS, the 2020 Economic Development Services Agreement previously adopted and
authorized by Ordinance No. 39 of 2019 is void; therefore, it is necessary to adopt new authorizing
legislation authorizing the Mayor to enter into a contract with the Cabot Chamber of Commerce;
subject to the approval of this governing body; and

Development Fund to have money available for the sole purpose of community and economic
development; and

services to the Chamber of Commerce as described within 2020 Economic Development Services
Agreement.

ARKANSAS, THAT:

Agreement, attached hereto as Exhibit “A” and incorporated herein as by this reference, for

for economic development in the City of Cabot.

SECTION 2: This governing body hereby determines that due to the circumstances stated
above, formal competitive bidding is deemed not practical and therefore waives the formal

competitive bidding requirement, as allowed by state law.

ORDINANCE NO. 2 OF 2020

AN ORDINANCE TO AMEND VARIOUS SECTIONS OF THE CODE OF CABOT,
CHAPTER 4 ANIMALS FOR THE CITY OF CABOT; AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES

WHEREAS, it is the intent of the City Council of the City of Cabot, Arkansas to amend the
Code of Cabot and adopt the new Animal Control regulations set forth below in an effort to
encourage the humane treatment of animals.

NOW THEREFORE BE IT ORDAINED BY THE CITY COUNCIL OF CABOT,
ARKANSAS THAT:

SECTION 1: Chapter 4, Animals, Article I. — In General, § 4-1. — Definitions
is hereby amended to add and/or modify the following definitions:

Community Cat - Any free-roaming cat that may be cared for by one or more residents of
the immediate area who is/are known or unknown; a community cat may or may not be feral.
Working Cat means any free-roaming cat that may or may not be feral and "works" for its
upkeep by hunting vermin, such as rodents and is cared for by an individual or business

proprietor.

Eartipping — The removal of the 14-inch tip of a Community Cat’s left ear, performed
while the cat is under anesthesia. The purpose of eartipping is to identify the Community Cat as

being sterilized and lawfully vaccinated for rabies.
SECTION 2: Chapter 4, Animals, Article I. — In General § 4-1. — Definitions

is hereby amended to delete the following definitions:

Feral cat caretaker means any person or organization, other than an owner, who provides

food, water, shelter or otherwise cares for a feral cat.

Feral cat colony means a group of cats that congregate as a unit. Although not every cat in a
colony may be feral, any non-feral cats that congregate with a colony shall be deemed to be a

part of it.

Feral cat colony caretaker means any feral cat caretaker who is approved by city animal

services to care for a feral cat colony.

Organization and Procedures of the Cabot City Council

(a) Regularly Scheduled Meetings

(i)

(ii)

(iii)

The City Council shall meet twice a month in regularly scheduled meetings. The first
meeting shall, unless otherwise provided, be on the first Monday of the month at 6:30
pm and the second meeting shall, unless otherwise provided for, be on the third
Monday of the month at 7:00 pm. Nothing in this section should be read to prohibit
the City Council, upon majority vote, from altering the location, date or time of a
regularly scheduled meeting provided proper notice is given to the public and the
media.

The City Council has made the following changes to regularly scheduled meeting times
to accommodate holidays in 2020: the second regularly scheduled meeting in February
shall occur on February 24, 2020 at 7:00 pm, and the first regularly scheduled meeting in

AN ORDINANCE TO APPROVE AN ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT SERVICES

understanding of the economic development needs, formal competitive bidding is not practical and
the City of Cabot wishes to waive competitive bidding; and

towards achievement of the stated public purpose of this agreement: new businesses opened; the
number of new utility hookups throughout the City, with an emphasis on commercial
development; new commercial properties under construction or completed; new jobs created; the
increase in sales or property tax revenue; ongoing negotiations with businesses for expansion,
relocation, or other new development in the interest of the City; identifying potential incentives
for new businesses and making recommendations to the City in regards to those incentives; and
any other like criteria which articulates similar measures for economic growth.
6.

City Has No Financial Interest in Chamber

understand that the City has no financial interest in the business of the Chamber, nor shall the

City be deemed or construed to be a partner, joint venture participant, or otherwise be interested
in the assets, or revenues earned or derived by the Chamber.
7.

Parties not to use Name or Credit of Other Party

purchase, any equipment, supplies or other things or materials of any nature whatsoever.
Likewise, the City shall not use the name or credit of the Chamber in purchasing, or attempting
to purchase, any equipment, supplies or other things or materials of any nature whatsoever.
8.

Chamber is Independent Contractor
The parties agree that in the performance of its obligations set forth in this Agreement, the

Chamber shall be deemed an independent contractor in every respect and shall take all steps at
its own expense, and pursuant to the use of its own materials and its method of operation, on
tasks requested by the City. The City does not and will not assume any responsibility for the
means by which, or the manner in which, the Economic Development Services provided by the
Chamber are accomplished. The Chamber is solely responsible for the method, content and
sequence of performance of the work set forth in this Agreement.
9.

Non-Assignment of Agreement
The Chamber shall not transfer or assign, or attempt to transfer or assign, this Agreement,

or the license or any of the rights or privileges granted within this Agreement, without the express
written permission of the City. The City is under no obligation whatsoever to grant any permission
to the transfer or assignment of this Agreement.
10.

Compliance with Law

City ordinances, and with all laws of the federal government and the State of Arkansas, including
particularly the Act, and including but not limited to, bans on discrimination on the basis of race,

sex, color, national origin, gender or disability, and to the extent applicable, State of Arkansas or
federal freedom of information laws.
11.

Disclaimer

pursuant to the Act, and in no way suggests that the City endorses or agrees with any position
taken by the Chamber, the Arkansas State Chamber of Commerce, the United States Chamber of
Commerce, or any affiliated group.
12.

Quarterly Reports
Not less often than quarterly, the President/CEO of the Chamber shall submit reports to the

Mayor and City Council. Each report shall include a statement of the specific criteria contained
in numbered paragraph 5 of this contract and an articulation of compliance as to each of those
criteria. Each report shall also detail other actions the Chamber has taken to further economic
development in Cabot including planning, marketing and strategic advice and counsel regarding
job recruitment, development, retention and expansion, and business and economic development
generally.

Audited Financial Statements

all Economic Development Services activity provided under this Agreement at the City’s request.
14.

Recapture Provision
Annually, the Chamber shall provide to the Mayor and to the Cabot City Council a written

financial accounting of the use of the moneys provided to the Chamber pursuant to this
Agreement, together with supporting documentation generally conforming to Arkansas
Legislative Audit's requirements and detailing the Chamber’s progress toward, or achievement
of, the specific criteria described herein. To the extent that criteria are not satisfied on an annual

basis, the City Council may, by adoption of a Resolution, formally demand the refunding of the

for the receipt and disbursement of such funds. All debits and credits to such account will be

Meetin:

The City Council shall meet in regular session on the third Monday of each month at 7:00 PM.
When a hoilday occurs on any such Monday, the regular meeting shall be held on the following
Mondaa at the same hour unless otherwise proivided by motion. The regular meeting time may
be rescheduled by the City Council in special circumstances, but when so done the change must
be made far enough in advance to allow normal public notifications.

Location

The place of City Council meetings shall be in the Cabot City Annex unless another place has
been previously set by the City Council.

Work Session

Work sessions provide Council Members the opportunity to meet with staff in order to inquire
about complex issues, discuss solutions and alternatives,and thhe finalize agenda. Work sessions
may be used by councilmembers to prepare for upcoming regular meetings. These meetings are
less formal and are often used for information gathering; no formal votes are taken.
However, it should be noted that work sessions are subject to the open meetings law.
DISCUSSION NEEDED ON VOTING—yes or no

Special Meetings

Special meetings may be called by three or more Council Members or the Mayor. Notification of
a special meeting, including specific items to be considered, shall be at least two hours prior to
the meeting.

Executive Session
An executive session may be requested by any member of the City Council. A majortiy vote of
by the City Council to convene in excecutive session. Executive sessions will be permitted only

for the purpose of considering the employment, appointement, promotion, demotion, disciplining,
or resignation or any public officer or employee.

Addition of Agenda Items at City Council Meeting

Any member of the City Council or the Mayor may add an item to the agenda. However, they
should strive to always have thier item/items included on the work session agenda. A new item
added to the Council Agenda after the work session meeting should only be considered if it
required immediate City Council action. The City Council may only place such new item on the
City Council meeting’s agenda by suspending the rules by two-thirds vote.

Readings

suspend the rules.

If the emergency clause is requested, the reason shall be clearly stated witin the “emergency
clause” section of the ordinance, or it will not be considered by Council.

Council Committees

Each Council Committtee shall have three or four members each, newly appointed January off
each year. Appointments shall be per written request to the City Attorney, Council Member shall
list his/her top three committtee. When appointments are made should there be any conflict,
senority shall prevail. Every Council Member shall serve on a minimum of one committee. Each
committee shall elect a chair and vice chair during the first committee meeting.

committee to attend. In order for a committee to make an official recommendation to the City

Members who are not of the particular committee meeeting, but are in attendance, shall do so

10. Mayor Realtionship

In exercising its management responsibilities, the City Council reserves its authority to
approve policy which represents broad statements of its intentions, approves plans and
programs, and delegate authority of administration to the Mayor, except those rights
that are by law conferred upon or reserved to the city council. The City Council
delegates the authority of the Mayor to hire capable personnel within an approved
wage and salary policy, to plan and establish schedules and to train, supervise and
terminate employees. Per A.C.A. § 14-42-110, the City Council reserves the authority to
review the hiring or removal of a department head and may overturn the hiring or
removal of a department head by the Mayor upon two-thirds majority of the total
membership of the City Council

Definition of responsibilities.

(1) The Mayor has the principal responsibility for directing the operations of the city
government and for advising and assisting the City Council in its deliberations. In
connection with the latter responsibility, the City Council expects and requests the Mayor to
furnish it with whatever data, information, and material it may need to properly carry out its
functions in an informed manner.

disciplinary measures are taken against the responsible employee or employees.

11. City Council/Mayor Cooperation

Efficient management of the city can exist only through mutual understanding and complete
cooperation between the City Council and the Mayor. The Mayor's performance cannot be of

City Council Meetings

1. Regular Meeting

The City Council shall meet in agenda session on the third Monday of each month at 6:30
p-m. and meet in Regular session immediately following the agenda session. When a
holiday occurs on any such Monday, the regular meeting shall be held on the following
Monday at the same hour unless otherwise provided by motion. The 6:30 p.m. agenda
meeting shall be prior to the city council meeting at 6:30 pm. The agenda meeting is to
finalize our agenda prior to the meeting. At this time, Council could remove or add agenda
items. If the Mayor or Staff wish to add any items which had not been on the Committee
Work Session Tentative Agenda, and/or had not been placed on the City Council Tentative
Agenda, such items shall only be placed on the City Council Final Agenda with a 2/3 vote
of full Council. Council Members shall be allowed to place items on the Final Agenda at
any time.

2. Location

The place of City Council meetings shall be in the Cabot City Annex unless another place
has been previously set by the City Council.

3. Council Committee Work Session

All Work Session Agenda Meetings will be held the 18‘ Monday of every month at 6:30
p.m. Work sessions allow Council Committees to hold joint meetings and the opportunity
to meet with staff in order to inquire about complex issues, discuss solutions and
alternatives. Each Committee Chair shall call his/her Committee to order and shall preside
over his/her Committee’s meeting. Council members who are not members of particular
committee may participate the meeting, except for voting on committee recommendations.
In order for a Committee to make an official recommendation to city council, a majority of
the committee must agree on that recommendations. Absolutely no legislation shall be
approved at council committee meetings. Individual committee meetings shall hold as
needed.

4. Special Meetings

Special meetings may be called by three or more Council Members or the Mayor.
Notification of a special meeting, including specific items to be considered, shall be at least
two hours prior to the meeting.

5. Executive Session

An executive session may be requested by any member of the City Council. A majority
vote of by the City Council to convene in executive session. Executive sessions will be
permitted only for the purpose of considering the employment, appointment, promotion,
demotion, disciplining, or resignation or any public officer or employee.

6. Tentative Agenda Items

The City Council’s Committee Work Session Tentative Agenda shall be coordinated by
the Mayor’s office. All items for discussion or action at the regular council meeting shall
be included on the Tentative Agenda. A complete packet with all supporting documents
shall be provided to city council members prior to the city council committee work session.

The City Council’s agenda shall be coordinated by the Mayor’s office. All items for
discussion or action at the regular council meeting shall be included on the Tentative
Agenda. A complete packet with all supporting documents shall be provided to City
Council Members prior to the City Council Meeting.

A complete packet is to be distributed to each council member by 4:00 pm Thursday prior
to the Committee Work Session Meeting, as well as, 4:00 pm Thursday prior to the City
Council Meeting. If not received by close of day Thursday prior to either meeting the City
Council may cancel the meeting.

Any member of the City Council or the Mayor may add an item on the City Council
Committee Work Session Agenda, supporting documents and correspondence must
accompany all agenda items. City Council Members shall be allowed to place items on
agendas at any time.

7. Filing an Ordinance or Resolution

The city council, by resolution, shall determine the date and time ordinances and
resolutions must be submitted to the City Attorney’s office in order that the staff shall have
sufficient time to prepare all relevant information with each ordinance and/or resolution
for presentation to the city council.

to suspend the rules. If the emergency clause is requested, the reason shall be clearly stated

of a department head and may overturn the hiring or removal of a department head by the

WHEREAS, on or about January 14, 1963 the City of Cabot, Arkansas (the

all business incidental to or connected with the conducting of a Telephone business in
exchange for an annual payment from the Company to the City; and

WHEREAS, CenturyTel of Arkansas, Inc. d/b/a CenturyLink (the “Company”)

WHEREAS, Arkansas Code § 14-200-101 authorizes municipalities to require
telecommunications service providers to pay a franchise fee to operate within the local
government boundaries; and

WHEREAS, the City and Company have agreed to amend Ordinance No. 1-1963
to change the annual payment made to the City.

NOW THEREFORE, BE IT ORDAINED, that the Mayor and Council of the
City of Cabot, Arkansas hereby amend Ordinance No. 1-1963 to change the quarterly
payment made to the City subject to the following conditions the Company and the City
have previously agreed:

SECTION 1: That, Section 7 of Ordinance No. 1-1963 is hereby amended to
increase the current payment from two percent (2%) of its gross revenues to four and one
quarter percent (4.25%) to be paid quarterly to City.

EXECUTIVE ORDER CONCERNING THE ENFORCEMENT OF ZONING
REQUIREMENTS AND RELATED REGULATIONS

WHEREAS, formal emergencies have been declared at the national, state, and local levels
due to concerns over the global pandemic caused by the COVID-19 virus.

WHEREAS, the Mayor has the ex-officio authority to direct enforcement measures of the
City’s zoning requirements and other related regulations.

WHEREAS, the State of Arkansas has issued a directive prohibiting dine-in eating at
restaurants, and the Mayor of Cabot, in partnership with the Cabot City Council, wishes to provide
economic relief to both the businesses and their employees, as well as to members of the public in
providing them additional places to shop for needed food and goods

THEREFORE I, KEN KINCADE, MAYOR OF CABOT, DO HEREBY ORDER
AS FOLLOWS:

SECTION 1: I am hereby suspending enforcement of certain zoning requirements and
other regulations to allow Cabot restaurants to sell food, prepared meals, ingredients, cleaning
supplies, paper goods, and other sundries on their premises. Such items may also be delivered to
the public without need for further local permit. This suspension of enforcement will be subject
to the following conditions:

1. All business owners are responsible for ensuring that social distancing and other
health and safety precautions are followed to the greatest extent possible.

2. All businesses remain subject to all other state and federal laws, regulations, and
directives.

3. The suspension is subject to any other orders, regulations, or directives which may be
issued at the state or federal level in regards to the COVID-19 pandemic. Those
directives shall control to the extent they may conflict with this order.

4. The suspension will remain in effect until June 1‘, 2020, unless otherwise extended
by the Mayor, due to COVID-19, but no longer than December 31, 2020.

SECTION 2: This order confers no permanent right or entitlement on the restaurants
affected.

SECTION 3; This Order is being put in place after consulting the Cabot City Council via
public meeting on March 30, 2020 and in partnership with that body. Together we hope that this
Order will facilitate economic relief for businesses that are vital to our community and help
provide continued employment for their employees. We further hope that it will be beneficial to
the citizens of Cabot to have additional places to buy food and other goods during these difficult
times.

City Council Meetings
1. Regular Meeting
The City Council shall meet at in agenda session on the third Monday of each month at
6:30 PM. and meet in Regular session immediately following the agenda session. When a holiday occurs
on any such Monday, the regular meeting shall be held on the following Monday at the same hour unless
otherwise provided by motion.
The 6:30 PM AGENDA MEETING - the Agenda meeting shall be prior to the city council meeting at
6:30 pm. (This change, if approved by Council, would have to be advertised to the public and wound
be the only time change). The agenda meeting is to finalize our agenda prior to the meeting. At this
time, Council could remove or add agenda items. If the Mayor or Staff wish to add any items which
had not on the Committee Work Session Tentative Agenda, and/or had not been forwarded to the City
Council Tentative Agenda, such items shall only be placed on the City Council Final Agenda with a 2/3
vote of full Council. Council Members shall be allowed to place items on the Final Agenda at any time.
2.

Location
The place of City Council meetings shall be in the Cabot City Annex unless another place has been previously
set by the City Council.

3.

Council Committee Work Session

*****

Work sessions allow Council Committees to hold joint meetings and the opportunity to meet with staff
in order to inquire about complex issues, discuss solutions and alternatives. Each Committee Chair
shall call his/her Committee to order and shall preside over his/her Committee’s meeting. Council
members who are NOT MEMBERS of particular committee may participate the meeting, EXCEPT
FOR VOTING ON COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS. In order for a Committee to make
an official recommendation to city council, a majority of the committee must agree on that
recommendations. ABSOLUTELY NO LEGISLATION SHALL BE APPROVED AT COUNCIL
COMMITTEE MEETINGS.
INDIVIDUAL COMMITTEE MEETINGS SHALL HOLD AS
NEEDED.
4.

Special Meetings
Special meetings may be called by three or more Council Members or the Mayor. Notification of a special
meeting, including specific items to be considered, shall be at least two hours prior to the meeting.

5.

Executive Session
An executive session may be requested by any member of the City Council. A majority vote of by the City
Council to convene in executive session. Executive sessions will be permitted only for the purpose of
considering the employment, appointment, promotion, demotion, disciplining, or resignation or any public
officer or employee.

6.

Tentative Agenda Items
The City Council’s Committee Work Session Tentative Agenda shall be coordinated by the Mayor’s
office. All items for discussion or action at the regular council meeting shall be included on the
Tentative Agenda. A complete packet with all supporting documents shall be provided to city council
members prior to the city council committee work session.

The City Council’s agenda shall be coordinated by the Mayor’s office. All items for discussion or action
at the regular council meeting shall be included on the Tentative Agenda. A complete packet with all
supporting documents shall be provided to City Council Members prior to the City Council Meeting.
A complete packet is to be distributed to each council member by 4:00 PM Thursday prior to the
Committee Work Session Meeting, as well as, 4:00 PM Thursday prior to the City Council Meeting.
If not received by close of day Thursday prior to either meeting Council may cancel the meeting.
Any member of the City Council or the Mayor may add an item on the City Council Committee Work
Session Agenda, supporting documents and correspondence must accompany ALL agenda items. City
Council Members shall be allowed to place items on agendas at any time.
7.

Filing an Ordinance or Resolution
The city council shall determine the date and time by resolution, such ordinances and resolutions must
be filed with the City Attorney’s office in order that the staff shall have sufficient time to prepare all
relevant information with each ordinance and/or resolution for presentation to the city council.

8.

Readings
All ordinances shall be read aloud at three different meetings unless the City Council votes to suspend the
rules. If the emergency clause is requested, the reason shall be clearly stated within the “emergency
clause” section of the ordinance, or it will not be considered by Council.

9.

Council Committees
Each Council Committee shall have three or four members each, newly appointed January or each year.
Appointments shall be per written request to the City Attorney, Council Member shall list his/her top three
committee. When appointments are made should there be any conflict, seniority shall prevail. Every Council
Member shall serve on a minimum of one committee. Each committee shall elect a chair and vice chair during
the first committee meeting.

10. Mayor Relationship
In exercising its management responsibilities, the City Council reserves its authority to approve policy which
represents broad statements of its intentions, approves plans and programs, and delegate authority of
administration to the Mayor, except those rights that are by law conferred upon or reserved to the city council.
The City Council delegates the authority of the Mayor to hire capable personnel within an approved wage
and salary policy, to plan and establish schedules and to train, supervise and terminate employees. Per A.C.A.
§ 14-42-110, the City Council reserves the authority to review the hiring or removal of a department
head and may overturn the hiring or removal of a department head by the Mayor upon two-thirds
majority of the total membership of the City Council
Definition of responsibilities.
(1) The Mayor has the principal responsibility for directing the operations of the city government and
for advising and assisting the City Council in its deliberations. In connection with the latter
responsibility, the City Council expects and requests the Mayor to furnish it with whatever data,
information, and material it may need to properly carry out its functions in an informed manner.
(2) The Mayor also has the principal responsibility to ensure that the city's administrative officers and
department heads understand and obey all local, state, and federal laws pertaining to the city's
operations, and when a violation of any law is discovered, that immediate disclosure is made to the City
Council and proper and adequate disciplinary measures are taken against the responsible employee or
employees.

11. City Council/Mayor Cooperation
Efficient management of the city can exist only through mutual understanding and complete
cooperation between the City Council and the Mayor. The Mayor's performance cannot be of the best
unless he is given the latitude to exercise independent judgment in executing policies of the City
Council. The City Council acknowledges that obligation and gives the Mayor the latitude of judgment
and discretion, and expects faithful performance in carrying out the policies of the City Council.
It shall be understood that administrative authority for the management of the city rests with the Mayor.
Members of the City Council should refrain, as individuals, from giving specific direction or instruction
to city personnel pertaining to the discharge of assigned duties, however, open communication between
aldermen and city employees is encouraged and expected to guarantee sound decisions based upon the
free flow of information.

December 2019 Financials were presented. GREG SLED MOTIONED TO ACCEPT THE
DECEMBER 2019 FINANCIALS AS PRESENTED, SECOND BY TRICIA AMBREAU. We had a better
month than it looks like on paper. Grant money was paid out this month. Ended the month by

rescheduling fourteen regular season games because of rain, we would have made $100,00.00
if the games were played. The contract with Pepsi will expire in 2020. General Director Travis
Young explained that he is putting out an RFP (Request for Proposal) to all the major beverage
companies in our serve area. ALL VOTED AYE, MOTION PASSED.

Program Director Lorenzo Mendoza reported youth programs. Basketball is currently being
played and going well. Youth Spring sports registration began this past week. The number of
those registered is up from last year figures during the early bird registration. Registration ends
on February 20th followed by tennis registration. The youth Spring sports will all begin in March.

napkins that had the logo on it. She said that it was a very successful event. Because of the sponsorships that they received, they
had 120 airmen attend for free.
Cabot City Beautiful – Matt Webber was here to talk about the Cabot Christmas Parade. He said that with the route, date & time
change, that the parade was a huge success. Of the $10,500 that the A&P funded, they spent the money on liability insurance,
mobile light unit, trophies, checks to all high school bands that participated and porta-potties. They are returning a check for
$1,961.05 for funds not used.
Cabot’s Christmas Celebration. Matt said that it was a fantastic event. They had hotdogs that Regions Bank grilled and ran out
of. They started with 500. Porchlight Realty had a hot cocoa station. The high school came out and did crafts with the kids. Santa
was able to stop and visit with the kids. Of the $10,000 received from the A&P Commission, the funds were used for various
decorations for the city hall area and the tree lights, Cockrill Country Critters for the live nativity scene, refreshments and Christmas
tree ornaments, They returned a check in the amount of $3,784.57 for funds not used.
Cabot Foundation for Arts and Culture – John Rudd and Rebecca Williams were here. Of the $50,000 received from the A&P
Commission, $46,000 was to be used for the McClure Placemaking Plan and $4,000 for fundraising. He attached copies of the
checks written to McClure, and all $46,000 was used. Of the $4,000 for fundraising, they only used $706.00 and gave us a check
back for $3,293.98 for the unused funds. You can check out their website at cabot2025.com to see all that they are doing. They did
12 vision sessions. They had input from the community. In the placemaking plan, they said that Cabot could use a new branding,
and they have given them to the mayor to go through and fine tune it. The citizens said that they wanted more festivals. John said
that Cabot has two amazing festivals already and now they are going to do neighborhood festivals, kind of like block parties. The
“crown jewel” is a revitalization of the old firehouse. It will host several different things. John said it would drive tourism, help our
citizens and make an impact on the economic growth of Cabot. “It would host an art gallery so that we can host local artists.” There
will be a coffee bar and a restaurant. It would include a performance stage. There will be classes in the back half of the firehouse.
Classes like photography, culinary, painting, stain glass. They have created a capital campaign committee that will help raise funds
for this center. They are looking at about 2 years out before they can start work on the old firehouse, if city council supports it.
Looking at construction hopefully starting around the first part of 2021. This will cost around $600,000.
110

Master Gardners – Caroline Bonifant and Katie Zhare were here. They brought photos for everyone to see. Their latest project
was to keep up the highway sign. They have a crew of 8-10 people to help keep that up. They put in some magnolias, knockout
roses and plants that will be great and very hearty out in the hot sun. They change out the décor year-round, like putting out mums
in the fall. They also won a project of the year award for their work in Cabot.
Cabot Athletics – Scott Reed and Kasey Wylie were here to give the recap. They were given 5,650.00 for the 6A State Volleyball
tournament. They explained that it was a first-class event. It was a 4-day event with 8 teams from NW AR, along with 4 Central
AR teams. With an average of 30 coaches, players and trainers per team, we had several in our town. We had signs and printed
programs with the A&P logo in it showing that they were a sponsor. They had several positive comments about the tournament.
Funding Request – Kathleen Ashmore was here from the Cabot Public Library asking for funding for the Summer Reading
Program. They partner with the Cabot Public Schools. This program is for kids to continue to read throughout the summer not to
lose what they have learned in school. She is asking for $5,000. After listening to the request. She is asking for the money to help
with the costs of the program. They focus on that each student takes home at least one book with them to read. The money would
go to awards for the kids completing challenges and supplies for the program. Judd Arnold asked how this was advertised.
Kathleen told him that they advertise through their social media aspects and flyers. The school district sends home flyers about it
also. Judd Arnold said that the A&P cannot pay for supplies. He told Kathleen that if she would amend the funding request and ask
for money for advertising and advertise that the Cabot A&P Commission is a sponsor, then the A&P could help. He said that we
could help promote it but could not pay for supplies. She said that she would amend her request and come back and thanked him for
his input. The commission decided not to fund this at this time the way it was presented.
Cabot Counts Census Committee – Mickey Spillane was here asking for $10,000. He explained that each person counted in Cabot
is worth $150 over a 10-year period. Mickey said that they are asking for funds to advertise inside and outside of Cabot. Judd
asked Mickey if he had gone to the city to ask for funding. Mickey explained that this all starts at the city level. He said that the
count Cabot committee started at the mayor’s office. He also explained that wherever you are on April 1 st is where you get counted,
so he wants as many people as possible to be in Cabot on April 1 st. Clint McGue spoke up and said that “the Cabot A&P would
have to decide if this would promote Cabot.” He said, “that monies from the A&P are not to create economic windfalls for
anybody, they are used to promote the city as a whole entity.” “These monies aren’t used to raise money.” Ed Long said that “of the
federal money that will come to Cabot through the census, the Cabot A&P Commission will not get any of it.” The commission
agreed that this would benefit Cabot but would not benefit the commission. Judd said that “as it is written that he doesn’t think that
the commission can fund it. If they were to get us a saying that would be on the billboard outside of town, then maybe the
commission could do something with that part.” Judd asked if there was a motion and nobody spoke up. It was not funded.
Judd Arnold said that “he was going to allow Cabot Foundation for Arts and Culture (CFAC) to present a small funding request
because of his concern that we may not have a quorum next month.” John Rudd said that Cabot2025 is because everything should
be completed and up and running. John said that murals drive tourism and community interaction. They are asking for a funding
request for 3 murals in the amount of $35,000. He showed a picture of the first mural and said that it would be completed by
Strawberry Fest. He said that people will get in front of it and take selfies and use hashtags that will help promote Cabot on social
media. He said that “the average cost of one this size is about $9,100. That includes their food allowance, putting them up in a
hotel, the paint and equipment. This paint, once done is sealed to protect it moving forward against graffiti. You can’t stop graffiti,
but it will make it easier to clean up and CFAC would stay on top of that.” They would like to paint a mural on the side of the old
firehouse on the wall in the alley. They also have other walls that Patrick Melikian has allowed them to use. They have in the
sample picture of the mural, “strawberry capital of Arkansas” They were asked if they can use that and John said that they are
having it checked out to see if they can use it or if it has been trademarked. Becky Williams said that “it is proven that if people
come to your town for arts and culture spend twice as much and stay twice as long as other tourists.” “Murals are an attraction that
bring people in and then they will spend money.” John said that “the mayor is part of this charge in support of the city council in
identifying the arts and entertainment district.” “Ultimately, these murals will be in or around this area to start, that is the epi
center.” “If they are city owned, we have permission to paint them.” Judd asked, “if the mayor would have to go through the city
council to get approval to paint the buildings?” “Both Ed Long and Norma Naquin, city councilmen said that “yes, he would have to
have city council approval.” Jay Lallu made a motion to approve the funding if the city council approves the walls. Ed Long and
Norma Naquin both abstained from voting since they are city council. John Rudd said that there is no shortage of walls to use and
that several business owners have offered their walls for murals. Ed said that if they could find a private wall for them to put the
first mural on, that would be absolutely just super-duper and fund the first one.” Judd said that the motion on the floor was to
approve the $35,000 pending the approval of public walls and approved by the city council and asked if that was correct.” Jay Lallu
agreed, as he was the one that made the initial motion. Brian Knowles made the 2 nd and all but Ed and Norma voted, and it passed.
111

Chamber Report – Gina Quattlebaum said that we had a great Christmas Open House. We had an awesome turnout for our annal
banquet with 49 tables. Lt. Governor Tim Griffin did great. We have sold all lanes for or Bowling for Business. This is as great
networking event. Our joint chamber luncheon with Jacksonville is coming up on March 17 th. On March 31st, we will have our
membership cookout appreciation day. We invite everyone to come so that we can show our appreciation.
Cabot Parks & Rec – Travis Young was here. He reported that the turf is in and that they have spent close to an extra $10,000 on
sod to re-sod several areas to fill ruts. They have either put down sod or re-seeded all fields. The community center is battling
leaks all over the place, so we are working on that. Basketball ends on Saturday and it has been a pretty good year. Wrestling is
coming along great. We started with 7 wrestlers and we are now up over 60 something kids. Spring sports registration has kicked
off. We are looking at over 2,000 to register. Travis also stated that it was his understanding that Cabot Parks & Rec is supposed to
get 75% of the A&P funds and they are actually only getting 62% not including add ons, Ed Long said that he drove the initiative to
get that done and that they settled on 75%. Judd Arnold said that with the add ons, that they are getting well over 75% of the A&P
budget. He also said that he wouldn’t put the turf, a $100,000 plus a year project in the add on category. He said that with that and
what he gets monthly, that he is getting well over 75%. Ed Long said that he looked closely at the numbers back in September and
it showed that Cabot Parks and Rec was actually, with add ons and everything, receiving around 92% of revenues.
General Discussion- Judd Arnold served as today’s chairman. It was discussed by the commission that he be appointed as the
A&P Chairman and all agreed. Judd Arnold introduced Greg Jones to the commission as a possible new commissioner. We had
two names recommended and they are Nelson Lively and Greg Jones. Since Nelson has part ownership in Dairy Queen, they feel
that Greg will be the better choice. Jay Lallu made the nomination to appoint Greg Jones to the commission at large position. Brian
Knowles 2nd it. Ed Long and Norma Naquin both abstained from voting. It passed.
Clint McGue mentioned there is a business that we continue to have issues with them not paying their taxes. It is a business that has
already closed, and they are working on getting it paid. Letters have gone out to those behind, so we are working on it.
The next A&P meeting will be March 17, 2020.
The motion to adjourn the meeting was made by Judd Arnold and a 2nd was made by Jay Lallu. The time was 10:25 a.m.

In response to the 2020 COVID-19 outbreak and restrictions placed on socia

by Mayor Kincade.

Ben Hooper, City Clerk & Treasurer Tammy Yocom and IT Director Roger Self.

4.9.1 Accessory Buildings

a. Permitting: An Accessory Building may be granted a building permit by the Administrative Official if
the following conditions are met:

iii. An Accessory Building may not be used for rental or commercial purposes.

iv.. No building shall be erected, placed or altered until the building plans, specifications, exterior
color scheme, and plot plan showing the location of such building with respect to existing
topography, lot lines, easements, building setbacks, and finished ground elevations have been

approved in writing by the City.

b. Accessory Building Limitations:

i. Building Area: The maximum combined area allowed for any and/or all detached accessory buildings
shall be:

a. lots one-half (0.5) acre or less, the combined square footage of all accessory buildings shall
be not more than half that of the principal building, with a maximum of eight hundred fifty
(850) square feet.

~ b. On lots larger than one-half (0.5) acres, the combined square footage of all accessory
buildings shall not be greater than five (5) percent of the total lot area, up to a maximum

ii. A detached accessory building in a residential district must be located behind the principal
structure, or on the rear one-half (1/2) of the lot at a distance not less than ten (10) feet from
any existing dwelling, or, any dwelling under construction on the same lot, or, on an adjacent
lot.

iii. Height for accessory buildings shall be measured from the bottom of the sole plate to the
underside of the roof deck and shall be governed as follows:

a. Lots one-half (0.5) acre or less shall have a maximum sidewall height of ten feet (10’).

b. Lots larger than one-half (0.5) acre shall have a maximum sidewall height of seventeen
feet (17°).

iv. The color of the Accessory Building shall be consistent with the colors of the main structure.

WHEREAS formal emergencies have been declared at the national, state, and local levels
due to concerns over the global pandemic caused by the COVID-19 virus.

WHEREAS the Mayor has the ex-officio authority to direct enforcement measures of the

WHEREAS the State of Arkansas has issued a directive prohibiting dine-in eating at
restaurants and other businesses have likewise suffered a financial downturn due to the emergency
circumstances, the Mayor of Cabot wishes to provide economic relief to both the businesses and
their employees through encouraging Cabot residents to patronize local businesses.

THEREFORE I, KEN KINCADE, MAYOR OF CABOT, DO HEREBY ORDER
AS FOLLOWS:

SECTION 1: Iam hereby suspending enforcement of certain sections of the City’s sign
code to allow local businesses to encourage Cabot residents to shop local. This suspension of
enforcement will be subject to the following specifications and conditions:

1. This waiver of enforcement specifically allows Cabot businesses to display temporary
signs that would not normally be allowed under the City’s sign code to encourage
Cabot residents to shop local.

2. All signs displayed pursuant to this order must be specifically purposed to encourage
Cabot residents to shop local.

3. The City reserves the right to require the removal of any signs that do not comply
with the sign code and are not appropriately advancing this order’s stated purpose or
are not otherwise in the best interest of the City.

4. The suspension will remain in effect until June 1‘, 2020.

SECTION 2: This order confers no permanent right or entitlement to the businesses who
take advantage of it. Any signs not in compliance with the City’s sign code will have to be
removed immediately upon expiration or withdraw of this order.

SECTION 3: The Order is being put in place after consulting with the Cabot City
Council via public meeting. Together we hope that this will encourage Cabot residents to shop
local, facilitate economic relief for businesses that are vital to our community, and help provide
continued employment for those businesses’ employees during these difficult times.

ITIS SO ORDERED

Maggie Cope called the meeting to order at 6:30 pm.

JOHN C. THOMPSON MOTIONED TO AMEND THE AGENDA, SECOND BY GREG SLED, ALL SAY
AYE.
The commission will continue discussion of the COVID 19 virus from the special meeting on
March 15th. All youth sports have been suspended. The community center is still open for
business. Anna Haver and Carey Woods with the State Health Department were present to
answer question about the COIV-19 virus. The average number of people visiting the
community center is about 20 to 30 at any given time in a space of 30,000 square feet, which
makes us in compliance with CDC guidelines. General discussion was about the CDC guidelines
for washing hands and sanitizing hard surfaces including equipment. The recommendation was
to post the guidelines for the public to read. There is no recommendation for closing the
facilities at this time and these recommendations will not supersede local recommendations.
General Director Travis Young stated that we have received 16 cases of EPA hospital grade
wipes that will be used to sanitize equipment and hard surfaces including counters and
doorknobs. Staff will continually wipe surfaces throughout open hours of the center. Patrons
will be asked to wash hands before and after facility usage. Signs will be posted encouraging
washing hands and to stop and not enter if you have any symptoms of the virus. Patrons will
also be asked to practice social distancing by not using equipment next to each other. Practicing
good hygiene and watching how we interact with each other will slow the spread. The health
department representative suggested putting all the CDC guidelines in place and require
patrons to follow these guidelines. Nick Whitaker would like to revisit the motion that he made
at Sunday’s meeting to suspend all day passes and not just those under the age of 18.
Suspending basketball pickup games was discussed. Maggie stated that she has been in contact
with the Mayor through email. The Mayor trusts that the commission will make the correct
choices as to the day to day operation of the parks department. The busiest hours in the center
were discussed and when is the best time to disinfect. Changing hours of operation is a
possible option. Discussion led to how long and on what surfaces the virus survives. There is no
evidence that atmospheric conditions, moisture in the pool area or dry air in other areas, have
an effect on the virus viability to thrive. Physical activity is so important to promote health and
keeping up with current recommendation is the best option. The government is not permitted
to take a person’s temperature due to HIPPA law. The fitness equipment in the fitness center is

4.9.1 Accessory Buildings
a. Permitting: An Accessory Building may be granted a building permit by the Administrative Official if
the following conditions are met:
i.

The building is not designated for full time occupancy and it has no sleeping quarters.

ii. The Accessory Building may be a pre-fabricated design, arriving as a fully assembled structure.
iii. An Accessory Building may not be used for rental or commercial purposes.
iv. No building shall be erected, placed or altered until the building plans, specifications, exterior
color scheme, and plot plan showing the location of such building with respect to existing
topography, lot lines, easements, building setbacks, and finished ground elevations have been
approved in writing by the City.
b. Accessory Building Limitations:
i.

Building Area: The maximum combined area allowed for any and/or all detached accessory buildings
shall be:
a. lots one-half (0.5) acre or less, the combined square footage of all accessory buildings shall
be not more than half that of the principal building, with a maximum of eight hundred fifty
(850) square feet.
b. On lots larger than one-half (0.5) acres, the combined square footage of all accessory
buildings shall not be greater than five (5) percent of the total lot area, up to a maximum
of three thousand, five hundred (3,500) square feet

ii. A detached accessory building in a residential district must be located behind the principal
structure, or on the rear one-half (1/2) of the lot at a distance not less than ten (10) feet from
any existing dwelling, or, any dwelling under construction on the same lot, or, on an adjacent
lot.

underside of the roof deck and shall be governed as follows:
a. Lots one-half (0.5) acre or less shall have a maximum sidewall height of ten feet (10’).
b. Lots larger than one-half (0.5) acre shall have a maximum sidewall height of seventeen
feet (17’).
